prize_parts.citation: for building the intertemporal, microfounded framework of open-economy macroeconomics and for identifying the exchange-rate disconnect puzzles that continue to organise the field

statement.case_for: Obstfeld and Rogoff turned international macroeconomics into a field where exchange rates, current accounts and welfare are analysed with explicit intertemporal microfoundations. The Redux model and the 1996 textbook became the template for the open-economy models used in central banks and international institutions. These models carry nominal rigidities and are now the standard policy apparatus. The disconnect and PPP puzzles are a durable empirical agenda that still sets research priorities. The attribution is compact: two names, a long joint record, and a shared framework and book. The work is about thirty years old and has been thoroughly absorbed, so timing is not a concern. Having reread the other openings, I still find this the cleanest combination of breadth, durability and attribution on the shortlist. I would weight attribution cleanliness and demonstrated durability more heavily than the size of the current policy debate.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the contribution is as much a synthesis and organising framework as a single discovery. The puzzles it highlights, especially exchange-rate disconnect, are still unresolved, so the empirical half of the credit is open rather than confirmed. The framework also overlaps conceptually with the New Keynesian tradition, and other authors extended the open-economy models. Some colleagues may reasonably judge that a prize for a framework with open puzzles is less decisive than one for a body of work whose empirical findings have been tested and replicated, such as the labour-market candidate.

responses.point: Teorell ranks this entry low. He questions whether it is a framework rather than a discovery, notes that the empirical puzzles are only partly resolved, and points to credit for other open-economy contributors such as Sachs, Svensson and Lane.
responses.response: I concede that the empirical side is open, and the citation should rest on the framework, not on any claim that the puzzles are solved. The Academy has often honoured frameworks that changed how a whole field models its questions, and this one did that for open-economy macro. The disconnect puzzles show the framework's productivity, because they gave later work a precise target. The contributions of Sachs, Svensson, Lane and others are real, but the joint Obstfeld-Rogoff papers and textbook are the point where the microfounded framework was consolidated and diffused. I am not persuaded that unresolved puzzles should count against the pair, though I accept that they weaken any claim of a settled empirical result.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks the technology and trade-shock candidate first, on its credible designs, replication and policy influence. She also flags the attribution problem of choosing Katz or Dorn, the overlap of Katz's strand with Goldin's prize, and the omission of Acemoglu from the task framework.
responses.response: I agree this is a strong scientific case, and I ranked it second. The empirical designs have been widely emulated, and I do not discount it on quality. My difficulty is the same attribution problem she names. The skill-premium strand and the China-shock strand are separable contributions with partly different authors. The three-name cap leaves out Dorn, a co-author of the central trade-shock papers, and Katz's strand overlaps with a recent prize. The size and persistence of the trade-shock effects are also still debated. I would want the committee to decide first whether this is one discovery or two before it takes precedence over a pair whose joint credit is unambiguous. If it is judged a single coherent contribution, I regard it as the most serious competitor to my preference.

responses.point: Krusell ranks the collateral-constraint candidate first, citing a clean two-person attribution to Kiyotaki and Moore, nearly three decades of extension, and confirmation of relevance after 2007-09. He also notes the overlap with the 2022 prize and the weaker empirical identification.
responses.response: I share his view that Kiyotaki and Moore have the cleanest attribution of any macro candidate, and I keep it as an alternative. I place it behind the open-economy pair for two reasons. First, it sits closer to the banking and crisis ground recognised in 2022. Second, much of the empirical identification of collateral-driven amplification was done by others, using calibrated models, so the evidence for the mechanism is less direct than the theoretical influence. The open-economy framework has a broader reach across policy institutions, though I accept that this is a judgement and not a decisive scientific difference.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats the open-economy framework and the disconnect puzzles as one achievement or sees the unresolved empirical side as a reason to wait.
Whether the technology and trade-shock candidate would be judged one coherent discovery and, if so, how Dorn and Katz should be treated under a three-name cap.
How to weigh a framework-based contribution against candidates with more directly replicated empirical findings.
I rely on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Obstfeld or Rogoff is apparent from the supplied profile. The profile does show frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell and co-authorship with John Hassler, and I am an IIES colleague of both. Both are fellow committee members who have commented on the entries I discuss. I also have a long collaboration with Peter Klenow, a credited name on B031, which is not part of my preferred configuration. These connections are disclosed and not adjudicated.
